title: The Idea That Refused to Die: Part 1: From Bartlett to the Cognitive 'Revolution'
author: Marc Smith
summary: Smith traces the surprising history of schema theory, arguing it is one of psychology's most influential ideas despite decades in which almost no one discussed it. He begins with Frederic Bartlett's 1932 book Remembering, where Bartlett -- critical of Ebbinghaus's meaning-stripped memory experiments -- used folk stories, photographs, and drawings to show that people reconstruct memories from the familiar rather than storing exact traces, a finding that pointed away from the 'warehouse metaphor' of memory storage. Unable to find an existing theoretical vocabulary, Bartlett adapted the concept of 'schema' from his friend Henry Head, a neurologist who had studied brain-injured WWI soldiers and found the brain maintains a continuously updated 'postural schema' of the body's physical position. Smith notes the irony that Bartlett himself disliked the term 'schema,' calling it 'at once too definite and too sketchy' for failing to capture how past experience remains dynamically active in shaping new understanding. The essay, the first in a series, ends on a historical cliffhanger: just as Bartlett formulated the idea in 1932, behaviourism's rise pushed his work to the margins for decades, even as Cambridge, under Bartlett's direction, quietly kept mental-process research alive until cognitive psychology eventually rediscovered schema theory.
points: Bartlett's landmark finding, based on folk stories, photographs, and drawings rather than tightly controlled word lists, was that people reconstruct memories rather than retrieving them intact -- directly contradicting the 'warehouse metaphor' of memory as static stored traces.

The concept of 'schema' originated not in memory research but in neurology: Henry Head's work with brain-injured WWI soldiers led him to propose that the brain maintains a continuously updated 'postural schema' tracking the body's physical position.
Bartlett explicitly disliked his own chosen term, writing it was 'at once too definite and too sketchy' -- because it implies a fixed structure rather than an active, moving process.
Schema theory nearly vanished for decades after 1932 as behaviourism's rise actively discouraged investigation of any unobservable mental process, including memory.

As director of the Cambridge Psychological Laboratory, Bartlett ensured the department never became fully captured by behaviourism, quietly preserving a line of mental-process research that would later feed the cognitive revolution.
quotes: In his 1932 book Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology, Frederic Bartlett first introduced the notion of cognitive schemas (or schemata), a term he adapted from the work of his close friend and professional confidant Henry Head.

Rather than supporting the warehouse metaphor of memory, where static traces or images are stored in the brain, Bartlett's studies pointed towards a more complex and nuanced picture. His participants didn't recall the stimulus material exactly or within its entirety, but reconstructed the material.

If the brain uses biological schema to constantly track and adjust physical posture based on past movements, thought Bartlett, it must use a cognitive schema to track, adjust, and interpret new information and experiences based on past knowledge.
Despite this choice, Bartlett writes: 'I strongly dislike the term "schema". It is at once too definite and too sketchy' (page 201-202).
By 1932, Bartlett's ideas were becoming eclipsed by behaviourism. Behaviourism discouraged all that could not be directly observed.

Researchers at Cambridge never stopped studying mental processes; their emphasis just shifted. So when Bartlett published Thinking in 1958, it wasn't part of a cognitive revolution, but rather a continuation of what Cambridge had been doing all along.
